USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Continue negotiating firmly from a position of leverage while the window remains open, but resist the urge to close a deal prematurely. The US holds significant structural advantage — tariffs covering ~$250B of Chinese goods remain in place, China's manufacturing sector is contracting (PMI below 50 for 3 consecutive months, lowest since 2009), and allies are aligning on Huawei restrictions. Push hard on structural reforms (IP protection, forced tech transfer, subsidies, enforcement mechanism) rather than settling for purchase commitments alone.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The US is in an advantageous negotiating position. China's economy is deteriorating — manufacturing PMI fell to 49.4 in December 2018 (first contraction in 2+ years), new export orders at decade lows in February 2019, and the World Bank forecasts growth slowing to 6.2% in 2019. Meanwhile, the US economy, while slowing (Atlanta Fed Q1 GDPNow at 0.3%), had 2.9% growth in 2018 and 2.6% in Q4 2018. The tariff leverage is real: $250B of Chinese goods face US duties while China has retaliated on only ~$110B of US goods, creating asymmetric pressure. The Huawei/Meng Wanzhou situation (extradition proceedings approved March 1, hearing March 6) and allied 5G bans (Australia, New Zealand, UK restrictions) give the US additional non-tariff leverage. However, the threat reading is tempered by several risks: (1) Lighthizer's March 12 testimony that 'nothing is really done until everything is done' suggests gaps remain on enforcement and structural issues; (2) Trump's eagerness for a Mar-a-Lago signing summit risks accepting a weak deal heavy on purchases but light on structural reform; (3) Schumer's March 12 criticism that 'China is playing us' reflects bipartisan pressure for a strong deal; (4) US Q1 growth is tracking near stall speed, giving China leverage to wait. The optimal stance is continued firm negotiation — neither escalating tariffs (which would hurt the slowing US economy) nor prematurely conceding (which would waste the leverage).
key_factors: China manufacturing PMI contraction for 3 consecutive months
US tariffs covering ~$250B of Chinese goods vs China's ~$110B retaliation
Lighthizer 'final weeks' testimony March 12 but 'nothing done until everything done'
US Q1 2019 GDP tracking near zero (Atlanta Fed 0.3%)
Trump eagerness for Mar-a-Lago summit risks weak deal
Schumer bipartisan criticism of potential weak deal
China detaining two Canadians (Kovrig, Spavor) as retaliation — reputational cost

sources_cited.excerpt: The original 90-day tariff-hike deadline passes without an increase (already delayed on Feb 24).
Lighthizer told the Senate Finance Committee that negotiators are 'working more or less continuously' to reach a deal with China. 'Our hope is that we are in the final weeks' of negotiations.
China's factory activity contracted for the first time in over two years in December. The official PMI fell to 49.4, below the 50-point level.
Manufacturing activity contracted for the third consecutive month in February 2019. The official manufacturing PMI has reached its lowest levels since 2009.
The Atlanta Fed's GDPNow initial model estimate shows negligible growth for the first quarter — just 0.3 percent.
The Chinese have still yet to make written commitments to any of the core issues. The two sides did not sign an official agreement and the White House did not release details on any agreements.

CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Continue negotiating actively while holding firm against the US demand for a unilateral enforcement mechanism. Offer expanded purchase commitments (agriculture, energy, semiconductors) as a bridge to a deal, but reject any provision that allows the US to unilaterally reimpose tariffs without bilateral dispute resolution. Use the Huawei/Meng Wanzhou case as implicit leverage — Trump has signaled willingness to link it to the trade deal.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: China faces genuine but not existential pressure. The tariff threat is real: US tariffs already cover ~$250B of Chinese exports at 10-25%, and the delayed List 3 hike from 10% to 25% could still be triggered (timeline entry 2018-09-17, 2019-02-24). McKinsey estimates the narrow GDP impact at 0.5-0.8%, but indirect effects through export job losses and consumer confidence erosion could be larger. China's exports fell 4% YoY in December 2018, and the Shanghai Composite was down 16% since the trade war began. Growth forecasts for 2019 are around 6.2%, down from 6.5-6.6% in 2018.

However, several factors mitigate the threat. Trump delayed the tariff hike on Feb 24, signaling eagerness for a deal. Lighthizer told Congress on March 12 that negotiators are in the 'final weeks' and 'making headway' on the toughest issues. The US side is under domestic political pressure too — Schumer accused Trump of rushing into a 'weak' deal, and the US Chamber of Commerce insists on enforcement. This suggests the US needs a deal as much as China does, which gives Beijing negotiating leverage.

The critical red line is the enforcement mechanism. The US demands the right to unilaterally reimpose tariffs if it judges China has violated the agreement (NYT, March 9). China's Commerce Ministry has proposed a bilateral consultation process instead. Accepting unilateral US enforcement would effectively cede sovereignty over trade policy and create a permanent sword of Damocles — future administrations could invoke it at will. This is worth resisting even at the cost of prolonging the current tariff pain.

The action stance of -0.1 (negotiate, slightly firm) reflects: (a) the situation warrants continued engagement since a deal is within reach, (b) China should not escalate given its economic vulnerability, but (c) China must not concede on the enforcement mechanism, which is a structural sovereignty issue. China's best play is to offer substantial purchase commitments — which Trump values politically — while holding the line on structural reforms and enforcement. The Huawei case provides additional leverage: Trump explicitly said on Feb 22 he might intervene in the Meng case for a trade deal, giving Beijing a card to play.
key_factors: US tariffs cover ~$250B of Chinese exports; List 3 hike from 10% to 25% was delayed but remains a threat
Lighthizer says talks in 'final weeks' as of March 12 — deal is close but gaps remain on enforcement
US demands unilateral tariff reimposition rights; China proposes bilateral consultation process
China's exports fell 4% YoY in Dec 2018; GDP growth forecast down to ~6.2% for 2019
Huawei/Meng Wanzhou extradition proceedings approved March 1; Trump linked it to trade deal
China detained two Canadians (Kovrig, Spavor) in apparent retaliation for Meng arrest
US debt-to-GDP at 249%, 10Y Treasury yield fell from 3.23% to 2.61% — US also faces economic headwinds
Schumer and US business groups pressure Trump not to accept a 'weak' deal — US needs a deal too

sources_cited.excerpt: Trump directs USTR to finalize List 3: 10% tariffs on ~$200B of Chinese imports effective Sept 24, scheduled to rise to 25% on Jan 1, 2019.
Trump tweets that talks have made substantial progress and further delays the scheduled List 3 hike from 10% to 25%
US DOJ unseals fraud and sanctions-related charges against Huawei and Meng; US formally requests Meng's extradition from Canada
Lighthizer told the Senate Finance Committee that negotiators are 'working more or less continuously' to reach a deal with China. 'Our hope is that we are in the final weeks.'

The Trump administration has pressed China to accept an agreement allowing the United States to unilaterally reimpose tariffs if it concludes that China has not gone through with structural changes to its economy.

The narrow short-term GDP impact on China of the tariffs alone is modest, on the order of 0.5 to 0.8 percent of GDP. But if tariffs lead to job losses in China and then a decline in consumer confidence, the medium-term impact will be much, much greater.
China's latest real GDP data showed only a small decline, yet the reality is that the trade war is taking a toll. The latest data, for December 2018, showed a -4% year-over-year decline in exports.
